analysis.one_liner: Replaces the single consumer watchdog director with a five-member bipartisan commission.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote in the Senate and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), created after the 2008 financial crisis to police mortgages, credit cards, and other consumer loans, is run by one director. This bill would have replaced that director with a five-member commission — no more than three from one party — appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate, and would have required the chair to get the commission's approval before requesting money from Congress. The bill made no change to the bureau's actual rules or enforcement powers, only to who runs it. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Financial companies regulated by the CFPB — banks, credit card issuers, mortgage lenders, debt collectors, and payday and other high-cost lenders — benefit if the bill passes. A five-member commission with staggered terms and a party-balance limit makes aggressive rulemaking and enforcement harder to approve, and vacancies can stall action entirely. Commissions also tend to act more slowly and seek consensus, giving firms more room to negotiate or delay cases against them. The funding provision also removes a single director's independent channel to ask Congress for money.

how_it_helps.text: It replaces the single Director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau with a five-member commission appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate, serving staggered five-year terms.
It bars any one party from holding more than three of the five seats, so no administration could fully control the bureau.
It requires the chair to get the commission's approval before submitting any budget requests to Congress, taking that power away from a single official.
The changes would not take effect until July 16, 2018.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers who rely on the bureau for protection against predatory lending, discriminatory credit practices, and abusive debt collection pay the cost of slower, more deadlock-prone enforcement if the bill passes. When the watchdog needs a majority of five commissioners to act and seats sit vacant, complaints and rulemakings can sit unresolved for months or years.

drawbacks.text: Commission structures are the norm for other financial regulators like the SEC and FTC, and supporters argue a five-member bipartisan commission would make the bureau more stable and less dependent on one person's priorities.

The bill does not change any of the bureau's substantive powers, funding, or rules — it only restructures its leadership — so it would not by itself remove any consumer protection on the books; it would mainly make action slower and require consensus.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The strongest case for the bill is structural, not substantive: major financial regulators like the SEC and FTC are run by bipartisan commissions, and a commission could have given the consumer bureau more political legitimacy and insulation from a single director's agenda. But the bill changed nothing about the bureau's actual rules or authority — its entire effect was procedural, making consumer enforcement slower and easier to stall through staggered terms, party balance limits, and a group veto over funding requests. In a bureau whose whole job is acting quickly against financial firms that harm consumers, the main practical effect would have been less aggressive oversight. The bill also never received a hearing or vote, so it was never tested or refined.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill expired when that Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Senator Deb Fischer introduced the bill on April 3, 2014, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee.
Six Republican senators cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did.
The Banking Committee took no further action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and it died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The financial industry, which would have faced a slower, more deadlock-prone consumer watchdog, is better off that the bill died; consumers keep the single-director structure. The bill's supporters also lose nothing, since the CFPB's structure was unchanged.

for.name: Sen. Deb Fischer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to replace the CFPB Director with a five-member commission.

against.name: Sen. Tim Johnson
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill, so it never received a hearing or vote.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support; the Democratic-run Banking Committee never took the bill up.

industries.industry: Banks, lenders, and other financial firms regulated by the CFPB
industries.note: A five-member commission with staggered terms and a party balance limit makes sweeping rules and aggressive enforcement harder to approve, and vacancies could leave the bureau unable to act at all. Firms facing CFPB oversight of mortgages, credit cards, and collections would face a slower, more negotiable regulator.

industries.industry: Payday lenders, debt collectors, and other high-cost credit providers
industries.note: These firms face the most direct CFPB scrutiny and have the strongest interest in a watchdog that moves slowly or deadlocks. A commission structure raises the number of votes needed to pursue cases against them.
